MSK–SKIN · WEEK 14 · MAIN LECTURE 1

Anterior Arm & Cubital Fossa · Lecture Companion

Anterior Arm & Cubital Fossa · Source: Mindy Johnson, Ph.D., 25-slide course presentation
Open condensed factoid →Learning objectivesCubital fossa

Big picture

The anterior arm is primarily a flexor compartment. Its biceps brachii, brachialis, and coracobrachialis are closely associated with the musculocutaneous nerve. The brachial artery and median nerve descend toward the cubital fossa, where their positions relative to the biceps tendon are essential for clinical examination and dissection. The ulnar nerve leaves the anterior compartment to pass behind the medial epicondyle, while the radial nerve courses posteriorly and returns toward the lateral elbow.

Learning objectives · coverage map

  1. Bony landmarks, elbow articulations and fracture/radial-head clinical correlations
  2. Brachial fascia, septa, compartments, and neurovasculature
  3. Anterior-arm muscle attachments, nerve supply, actions and deficits
  4. Cubital fossa boundaries, layers, and contents
  5. Musculocutaneous, median, ulnar and radial nerve course; biceps reflex
  6. Brachial arterial branches, elbow collateral network, superficial/deep veins
  7. Long-head biceps tendinopathy and rupture
  8. Recognition of structures in anatomical and cross-sectional images

The source presentation provides the listed objectives on slide 2; fracture mechanisms, radial-head subluxation, lymphatic pathways and modality-specific CT/MRI teaching are not detailed in its subsequent slides. These gaps are explicitly labeled where discussed.

1 · Osteology: humerus, radius and ulna

Humerus: landmarks organized by region (slide 5)

  • Proximal: head; anatomical neck; surgical neck; greater/lesser tubercles; intertubercular (bicipital) sulcus.
  • Shaft: deltoid tuberosity (lateral) and radial/spiral groove (posterior).
  • Distal: capitulum (lateral), trochlea (medial), medial/lateral epicondyles, anterior radial/coronoid fossae, posterior olecranon fossa, and ulnar groove behind medial epicondyle.

Proximal radius and ulna (slide 6)

  • Radius: head, neck and radial tuberosity.
  • Ulna: olecranon, trochlear notch, coronoid process, radial notch and ulnar tuberosity.

Spatial model: humeral trochlea aligns with the ulnar trochlear notch; capitulum with radial head. The radial head also articulates with the radial notch of the ulna to permit rotation.

BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT
Fracture relationships (not explained on the slides): surgical-neck fracture → axillary nerve risk; humeral shaft/radial groove fracture → radial nerve risk; distal supracondylar fracture → brachial artery and median nerve risk; medial epicondylar injury → ulnar nerve risk. Radial-head subluxation (nursemaid elbow) commonly follows longitudinal traction on a child’s pronated forearm with displacement of the annular ligament. The slides list these topics as objectives but do not give these specifics.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which bone carries the biceps tendon distally, and which carries brachialis?

Biceps → radial tuberosity; brachialis → coronoid process and ulnar tuberosity.

2 · Fascia and arm compartments

Brachial fascia and the medial and lateral intermuscular septa partition the arm (slide 8). The lateral septum spans between the deltoid insertion and lateral epicondyle.

Anterior compartmentPosterior compartment
Biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis; chiefly flexion/supination and shoulder flexion/adduction. Brachial artery/veins, musculocutaneous and median nerves; ulnar nerve proximally.Triceps; primarily elbow extension. Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery with middle and radial collateral branches.

Course matters: the ulnar nerve crosses the medial septum to go posterior; the radial nerve pierces the lateral septum in its return toward the anterior/lateral elbow.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why does the ulnar nerve appear behind the medial epicondyle despite occupying the anterior arm proximally?

It pierces the medial intermuscular septum and enters the posterior side of the distal arm.

3 · Anterior arm muscles and functional testing

MuscleAttachments in slidesInnervationAction / test
Biceps brachiiShort head: coracoid process; long head: supraglenoid tubercle → radial tuberosityMusculocutaneousForearm supination and elbow flexion; resist supination and flexion
BrachialisDistal half of humerus → ulnar tuberosity and coronoid processMusculocutaneous and radial (as emphasized by lecture)Elbow flexion; test resisted elbow flexion
CoracobrachialisCoracoid process → middle third of humeral shaftMusculocutaneousShoulder flexion and adduction; resist those movements

Reasoning: biceps attaches to radius and can rotate it in supination; brachialis inserts into ulna and flexes elbow independent of forearm rotation. Musculocutaneous damage weakens elbow flexion/supination and shoulder flexion/adduction, with remaining contributions from other muscles.

CLINICAL CONNECTION
Bicipital (biceps) myotatic reflex: relax the arm, pronate passively, partially extend the elbow; place the examiner’s thumb on the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa and tap the thumb. It tests musculocutaneous nerve and C5–C6 levels (slide 12).
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A lesion causes reduced supination strength, elbow flexion weakness and reduced biceps reflex. Which nerve is implicated?

Musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6 for biceps reflex).

4 · Long-head biceps tendon disorders

ConditionLecture findingMechanistic connection
Long-head biceps tendinopathyAnterior shoulder pain and localized tenderness in the bicipital groove (slide 13)The long-head tendon runs in the intertubercular groove; inflammation at that site explains point tenderness.
Long-head tendon rupture“Popeye deformity” (slide 14)Chronic wear in the bicipital groove can result in tendon rupture between supraglenoid tubercle and proximal groove, allowing distal muscle-belly retraction.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Where would the lecturer expect point tenderness in long-head biceps tendinopathy?

Anterior shoulder over the bicipital (intertubercular) groove.

5 · Nerve routes through the arm

NerveCourse emphasizedClinical reasoning
MusculocutaneousLateral cord → pierces coracobrachialis → travels between biceps and brachialis → lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerveMotor deficits in anterior arm; sensory loss lateral forearm
MedianTravels with brachial artery into cubital fossa; no branches in arm/axillaAt risk where close to artery and distal humerus
UlnarAnterior arm → pierces medial septum → behind medial epicondyle, medial to olecranon; no arm/axilla branchesVulnerable at exposed medial elbow
RadialPosterior arm → pierces lateral septum → near lateral elbow and separates into superficial/deep branchesLinks posterior-extensor function to lateral elbow
EXAM TRAP
Median and ulnar nerves do not give branches in the arm according to this lecture. Passing through a compartment does not mean innervating its muscles.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which nerve pierces coracobrachialis, and what skin territory does its continuation supply?

Musculocutaneous → lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve → lateral forearm skin.

6 · Vessels, anastomosis, and venous return

Arterial tree (slides 20–21)

Axillary artery → brachial artery at the inferior border of teres major. The brachial gives profunda brachii (→ radial and middle collateral), superior ulnar collateral (with ulnar nerve behind medial epicondyle), and inferior ulnar collateral (in front of medial epicondyle); terminates into radial + ulnar arteries.

The elbow arterial anastomosis forms alternative routes around a moving/compressed joint, maintaining perfusion despite elbow position or reduced flow along one path.

Venous pathways (slide 22)

Superficial: cephalic, basilic, median cubital veins. Deep: radial + ulnar veins → brachial veins that accompany brachial artery; brachial veins combine with basilic vein to form axillary vein.

Pulse: brachial pulse is palpated on the anterior/medial side near the cubital fossa (derived from brachial artery position).

BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT
Venipuncture: median cubital vein is often selected because it is superficial; bicipital aponeurosis helps separate superficial venous structures from deeper brachial artery and median nerve. Lymphatics: superficial vessels often accompany superficial veins toward regional nodes, while deep lymphatics track deep vessels; these pathways were not detailed in the provided slides.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Which branches are terminal branches of brachial artery, and where does axillary become brachial?

Radial and ulnar arteries; at inferior border of teres major.

7 · Cubital fossa: boundaries, layers, contents

Boundary/layerStructure
Superior/baseLine connecting medial and lateral epicondyles
Medial borderPronator teres
Lateral borderBrachioradialis
Floor (deep)Brachialis and supinator
Roof (superficial)Brachial and antebrachial fascia; bicipital aponeurosis

Contents, lateral → medial: TAN = Tendon of biceps, brachial Artery (with veins), Nedian nerve. The radial nerve is additionally present more laterally and divides into superficial and deep branches (slide 25). Thus, TAN is not an exhaustive list of everything in the fossa.

MUST KNOW
TAN is the medial-to-lateral order reversed: tendon → artery → median nerve when reading lateral to medial. Radial nerve sits farther laterally; do not omit it from a complete contents answer.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Where is brachial artery relative to biceps tendon and median nerve in cubital fossa?

Brachial artery lies medial to biceps tendon and lateral to median nerve.

8 · Cross-sectional and clinical image recognition

The lecture directly includes a transverse arm section (slide 8), anatomy illustrations (slides 5–6, 18–25), and ultrasound with Doppler of the long-head biceps tendon (slide 13). Although learning objective 8 asks for X-ray, MRI and CT recognition, no dedicated X-ray, MRI or CT examples are provided in these slides. Do not mistake generic anatomical figures for those modalities.

Unlabeled-image checklist

  • On distal humerus: distinguish capitulum versus trochlea, coronoid versus radial fossa, medial versus lateral epicondyle.
  • On proximal forearm: distinguish radial head/neck/tuberosity versus olecranon/coronoid/ulnar tuberosity.
  • On arm cross section: identify humerus, brachialis, biceps, triceps, intermuscular septa and neurovascular bundles.
  • On anterior elbow: identify pronator teres, brachioradialis, biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve and lateral radial nerve.
  • On shoulder tendon sonography: identify tendon within bicipital groove and thickened sheath/increased vascularity in tenosynovitis.

Master these before moving on

  1. Muscle-to-bone logic: biceps inserts on radius and supinates; brachialis on ulna and primarily flexes elbow. This predicts examination findings.
  2. Three distinct nerve paths: musculocutaneous pierces coracobrachialis, median accompanies brachial artery, ulnar passes behind medial epicondyle.
  3. Elbow architecture: knowing lateral/medial landmarks makes nerve, vessel, and cubital fossa orientation much easier.
  4. TAN and radial nerve: memorize the TAN sequence, but know radial nerve is lateral to the trio.
  5. Collateral circulation: elbow arteries form redundant routes around a frequently flexed joint.

Most useful Step 1 bridges (selective)

  • Humeral shaft fracture → radial nerve → extensor weakness (outside-lecture clinical bridge).
  • Supracondylar injury → brachial artery / median nerve risk → perfusion and neurovascular assessment (outside-lecture clinical bridge).
  • Musculocutaneous nerve lesion → impaired biceps and brachialis action + lateral forearm sensory loss.
  • Long-head tendon inflammation → bicipital groove tenderness; rupture → Popeye deformity.
